abstract: The President : Ladies and gentlemen, before calling upon the speakers to pass a vote of thanks to Prof. Bozzoli, I am sure you would like me, on your behalf, to thank him for his paper to-night which has been to me, and I am sure to all of us, of absorbing interest. He has traced back the historical background of electrical engineering from its very beginning, in a way that I, personally, have never heard done before. It makes us realise, I think, that the beginnings from which our profession comes had their roots very far back, and that the light and heavy current men have intermingled their roots and branches right through the picture. I think, the inauguration of this light current section to-night has opened a new chapter in the work of this Institute.

Since the introduction of the selenium rectifier, the use of the copper-oxide rectifier has been restricted largely to modulators and demodulators, and to moving-coil instruments for a.c. measurement. In both these applications a change in the rectifier characteristics will be serious. Modern copper-oxide rectifiers for, these applications, made by improved processes, are artificially aged during production so their characteristics are stable and no subsequent ageing is to be expected.

articleTitle: Discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: P. Machanik : The art of telecommunications, now about 100 years old, was initially based on the transmission of pulses over single-wire lines. The intervening period has witnessed some remarkable results. Development has crowded on development and it has needed sound judgment to determine which systems of communication should be introduced because of the fear that in a few years they would be replaced by some new discovery. The original discoveries utilized simple techniques but successive developments became more and more complex and required staff of higher intelligence and training. The first telephones and exchanges installed in South Africa were crude affairs judged by modern standards, just as the first motor-car — the horseless carriage — looks strange against the high-powered streamlined vehicle of to-day. In the urgencies of the present moment we perhaps fail to realize how hard the struggle was to set out a policy in order to give the Union a modern and dependable system of communication. The engineers of an earlier generation than mine were beset by conflicting claims by the sponsors of many systems and had to make difficult decisions. We would be false to our profession if we believed that modern telecommunication practices have crystallized in their present form and that great changes are not in the offing. These changes will affect us to a greater extent than in the past when we had a relatively small plant. Within a few years' time we shall have half a million telephones in use and it will not be such a simple matter to alter our methods. Hence it behoves all of us who have entered this interesting electrical field to be ever-vigilant and far-sighted and it is ever increasingly necessary for the Department to follow up this desire by providing a sound laboratory system.

articleTitle: Discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Major G. A. Harvey : We in aviation circles, who are responsible for the provision and engineering of communication circuits and navigational aid facilities, have a requirement for the recording of air/ground radio-telephone transmissions. This requirement has several features which are peculiar, due to the circumstance under which we operate and consequently differs in many ways from the broadcasting aspect outlined by Mr Middleton. The necessity for recording these air/ground transmissions is due to the fact that the post-war trend in aviation communications between the aircraft and ground stations is to use radio telephone in place of manual morse continous wave telegraphy. In the latter case a longhand log record is kept of all messages. Thus in the case of an inquiry into say an accident complete records are available with legal standing. In the ease of radio telephony if the higher speed-message capabilities of the system are to be realised normal longhand methods of message recording are impossible. Hence some form of automatic recording is an essential requirement. For legal reasons the present longhand records are retained for 90 days and then destroyed. It is thus easy to see that a recording system with erasing facilities is particularly attractive, from the point of view of cutting down recurring expenditure. After 90 days the impression on the tape can be erased and the tape re-used.
